text: Disjunctivism (Hinton, Snowdon, McDowell) is most distinctively characterized by its denial that:
choices: a veridical perception and a subjectively indistinguishable hallucination share a common experiential element, a 'highest common factor'
hallucination is a genuinely possible mental occurrence
we ever perceive mind-independent objects directly, even in the best case
perceptual experience has any phenomenal character at all
explanation: The signature move of disjunctivism is to reject the common factor principle: subjective indistinguishability does not entail a shared mental component, so the good (perceiving) and bad (hallucinating) cases are metaphysically distinct kinds with no highest common factor. Option 1 misreads the view, which grants that hallucination occurs; option 2 states indirect realism's denial of direct perception, the opposite of disjunctivism's claim about the good case; option 3 attributes a denial of phenomenal character that no disjunctivist makes. Only option 0 names what the view denies.
